problems.problem: A positive integer $n$ is such that the numbers $2n + 1$ and $3n + 1$ are perfect squares. Can the number $5n + 3$ be prime?

Two right triangles are placed in the plane so that their medians drawn to the hypotenuses are parallel. Prove that the angle between some leg of one triangle and some leg of the other triangle is half the angle between their hypotenuses.
Find all functions $f(x)$, defined for all positive $x$ and taking positive values, which satisfy $f(x^y) = f(x)^{f(y)}$ for all positive $x$ and $y$.

Prove that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that, if an equilateral triangle with side $n$ is divided by lines parallel to its sides into $n^2$ equilateral triangles with side $1$, then among the vertices of these triangles one can choose $1993n$ points no three of which are the vertices of an equilateral triangle (not necessarily with sides parallel to the sides of the original triangle).
Find all quadruples of real numbers in each of which every number is equal to the product of some two other numbers of the quadruple.

The positive integers from $1$ to $1993$ are written in a row in some order. The following operation is performed on the row: if the number $k$ stands in the first place, then the first $k$ numbers of the row are rearranged in reverse order. Prove that after several such operations the number $1$ will necessarily stand in the first place.

In a tennis tournament, $n$ participants want to play doubles (two against two) matches so that each participant has every other participant as an opponent in exactly one match. For which $n$ is such a tournament possible?

Prove that if two rectangular boxes have equal volumes, then they can be placed in space so that every horizontal plane that intersects one of them also intersects the other, and in a polygon of the same area.
Positive integers $a$ and $b$ are such that the number $\frac{a+1}{b} + \frac{b+1}{a}$ is an integer. Prove that the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ does not exceed $\sqrt{a + b}$.

Inside a convex $100$-gon, $k$ points are chosen, $2 \le k \le 50$. Prove that one can mark $2k$ vertices of the $100$-gon so that all the chosen points lie inside the $2k$-gon with the marked vertices.

Two circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ touch externally at the point $F$. Their common tangent touches $S_1$ and $S_2$ at the points $A$ and $B$, respectively. A line parallel to $AB$ touches the circle $S_2$ at the point $C$ and meets the circle $S_1$ at the points $D$ and $E$.

Prove that the common chord of the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $BDE$ passes through the point $F$.

Real numbers are written in the cells of an infinite sheet of squared paper. Two figures are considered, each consisting of a finite number of cells. The figures may be translated parallel to the grid lines by an integer number of cells. It is known that for every position of the first figure the sum of the numbers in the cells it covers is positive. Prove that there exists a position of the second figure for which the sum of the numbers in the cells it covers is positive.

A sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n, \dots$ is given in which $a_1$ is not divisible by $5$ and for every $n$
$$a_{n+1} = a_n + b_n,$$
where $b_n$ is the last digit of the number $a_n$. Prove that the sequence contains infinitely many powers of two.

Functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are defined on the set of integers whose absolute value does not exceed $1000$. Denote by $m$ the number of pairs $(x, y)$ for which $f(x) = g(y)$, by $n$ the number of pairs for which $f(x) = f(y)$, and by $k$ the number of pairs for which $g(x) = g(y)$. Prove that $2m \le n + k$.

The altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ and $DD_1$ of a tetrahedron $ABCD$ meet at the centre $H$ of the sphere inscribed in the tetrahedron $A_1B_1C_1D_1$. Prove that the tetrahedron $ABCD$ is regular. (An altitude of a tetrahedron is the segment of the perpendicular dropped from a vertex to the opposite face, contained between this vertex and the plane of that face.)

Players $A$ and $B$ take turns moving a knight on a $1994 \times 1994$ chessboard. Player $A$ may only make horizontal moves, i.e. moves in which the knight moves to an adjacent row. Player $B$ may only make vertical moves, in which the knight moves to an adjacent column. Player $A$ places the knight on the square from which the game starts and makes the first move. Each player is forbidden to put the knight on a square on which it has already been in this game. The player who has no move loses. Prove that player $A$ has a winning strategy.
Can all the numbers $1, 2, 3, \dots, 100$ be terms of $12$ geometric progressions?
Prove that every function defined on the whole real line can be represented as the sum of two functions whose graphs each have an axis of symmetry.

Two points at distance $1$ are marked in the plane. It is allowed, after measuring with compasses the distance between two marked points, to draw a circle with centre at any marked point and with the measured radius. With a ruler one may draw the line through any two marked points. The intersection points of the constructed lines are marked as new points.

Let $C(n)$ be the smallest number of lines whose construction with compasses alone allows one to obtain two marked points at distance $n$, where $n$ is a positive integer, and let $RC(n)$ be the same with compasses and ruler. Prove that the sequence $C(n)/RC(n)$ is unbounded.
Prove that if all the angles of a convex polygon are equal, then at least two of its sides have lengths not exceeding the lengths of their neighbouring sides.

Prove that for every positive integer $a_1 > 1$ there exists an increasing sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ such that $a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \dots + a_k^2$ is divisible by $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_k$ for all $k \ge 1$.

On a merry-go-round with $n$ seats, a boy rode for $n$ sessions in a row. After each session he got up and, moving clockwise, moved to another seat. The number of seats of the merry-go-round that the boy passes when moving, including the one on which he sits down, is called the length of the move. For which $n$ could the boy have sat on every seat during the $n$ sessions, if the lengths of all $n - 1$ moves are distinct and less than $n$?

The altitudes of a tetrahedron meet at one point. Prove that this point, the foot of one of the altitudes and the three points dividing the other altitudes in the ratio $2 : 1$, counting from the vertices, lie on one sphere.

Non-constant polynomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ with leading coefficients equal to $1$ are given. Prove that the sum of the squares of the coefficients of the polynomial $P(x)Q(x)$ is not less than the sum of the squares of the constant terms of $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$.
Can the number obtained by writing the integers from $1$ to $n$ ($n > 1$) one after another in a row read the same from left to right and from right to left?

Several travellers move with constant speeds along a straight road. It is known that during some period of time the sum of the pairwise distances between them decreased monotonically. Prove that during the same period the sum of the distances from some traveller to all the others also decreased monotonically.
Prove that for $n \ge 5$ a cross-section of a pyramid whose base is a regular $n$-gon cannot be a regular $(n+1)$-gon.

Prove that if the numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m$ are nonzero and for every integer $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$ ($n < m - 1$)
$$a_1 + a_2 \cdot 2^k + a_3 \cdot 3^k + \dots + a_m \cdot m^k = 0,$$
then the sequence $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m$ contains at least $n + 1$ pairs of adjacent numbers of opposite signs.
Do there exist three positive integers greater than $1$ such that the square of each of them, decreased by one, is divisible by each of the others?

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AB = BC$) the angle bisector $CD$ is drawn. The line perpendicular to $CD$ through the circumcentre of triangle $ABC$ meets $BC$ at the point $E$. The line through $E$ parallel to $CD$ meets $AB$ at the point $F$. Prove that $BE = FD$.

Does there exist a finite set $M$ of nonzero real numbers such that for every positive integer $n$ there is a polynomial of degree at least $n$ with coefficients from $M$, all of whose roots are real and also belong to $M$?

All integers from $1$ to $100$ are written in a row in an unknown order. With one question about any $50$ numbers one can find out in what order these $50$ numbers are written relative to each other. What is the smallest number of questions with which one can certainly find out the order in which all $100$ numbers are written?

Solve in integers the equation
$$(x^2 - y^2)^2 = 1 + 16y.$$

The re-examination of the Council of Sages is held as follows: the king lines them up in single file and puts on each a cap of white, blue or red colour. Every sage sees the colours of the caps of all the sages standing in front of him, but does not see the colour of his own cap or of those standing behind him. Once a minute one of the sages must call out one of the three colours (each sage calls out a colour once). After this process ends, the king executes every sage who called out a colour different from the colour of his cap. On the eve of the re-examination, all one hundred members of the Council agreed on and devised a way to minimise the number of executed. How many of them are guaranteed to avoid execution?

Two circles meet at the points $A$ and $B$. A line through the point $A$ meets the first circle again at the point $C$ and the second at the point $D$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the arcs $BC$ and $BD$ not containing the point $A$, and let $K$ be the midpoint of the segment $CD$. Prove that the angle $MKN$ is a right angle. (One may assume that the points $C$ and $D$ lie on opposite sides of the point $A$.)

An $n \times n \times n$ cube is made of unit cubes. A closed non-self-intersecting polygonal line is given, each segment of which joins the centres of two adjacent unit cubes (cubes sharing a face). Call marked those faces of the unit cubes that are crossed by the given polygonal line. Prove that the edges of the unit cubes can be coloured in two colours so that every marked face has an odd number of sides of each colour, and every unmarked face has an even number of sides of each colour.

All possible quadratic trinomials of the form $x^2 + px + q$ are considered, where $p, q$ are integers with $1 \le p \le 1997$, $1 \le q \le 1997$. Which are more numerous among them: those having integer roots or those having no real roots?

A polygon, a line $l$ and a point $P$ on the line $l$ are given in general position (i.e. all lines containing the sides of the polygon meet $l$ at distinct points different from $P$).

Mark those vertices of the polygon for which the lines containing the two sides issuing from it meet $l$ on opposite sides of the point $P$. Prove that the point $P$ lies inside the polygon if and only if on each side of $l$ an odd number of vertices is marked.

The sphere inscribed in a tetrahedron touches one of its faces at the intersection point of its angle bisectors, another face at the intersection point of its altitudes, and a third face at the intersection point of its medians. Prove that the tetrahedron is regular.

In a rectangular box with an $m \times n$ base, where $m$ and $n$ are odd numbers, $2 \times 1$ dominoes are placed so that only a $1 \times 1$ square (a hole) in a corner of the box remains uncovered. If a domino is adjacent to the hole with its short side, it may be slid along itself by one cell, covering the hole (a new hole is then opened). Prove that by such moves the hole can be moved to any other corner.

Lines parallel to the axis $Ox$ meet the graph of the function $y = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$: the first one at the points $A$, $D$ and $E$, the second one at the points $B$, $C$ and $F$ (see the figure). Prove that the length of the projection of the arc $CD$ onto the axis $Ox$ equals the sum of the lengths of the projections of the arcs $AB$ and $EF$.

The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$, respectively. The points $A_2$, $B_2$, $C_2$ are the midpoints of the arcs $BAC$, $CBA$, $ACB$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the lines $A_1A_2$, $B_1B_2$ and $C_1C_2$ meet at one point.

A family $S$ of equilateral triangles is drawn in the plane, obtained from each other by translations, and any two of the triangles intersect. Prove that there exist three points such that every triangle of the family $S$ contains at least one of them.

In the country N there are $1998$ cities, and from each of them there are non-stop flights to three other cities (all flights are two-way). It is known that from any city one can fly to any other, possibly with several changes. The Ministry of Security wants to declare $200$ cities closed, no two of which are joined by a flight. Prove that this can be done so that one can fly from any non-closed city to any other without changing planes in closed cities.

Inside the parabola $y = x^2$ there are distinct circles $\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \dots$ such that for every $n > 1$ the circle $\omega_n$ touches the branches of the parabola and touches the circle $\omega_{n-1}$ externally (see the figure). Find the radius of the circle $\omega_{1998}$, given that the diameter of $\omega_1$ is $1$ and that it touches the parabola at its vertex.

Do there exist $1998$ distinct positive integers such that the product of any two of them is divisible by the square of their difference?
Two non-intersecting spheres of diameter $1$ can be placed in a tetrahedron $ABCD$ all of whose edges have length at most $100$. Prove that one sphere of diameter $1.01$ can be placed in it.

A grid figure $\Phi$ has the following property: for any filling of the cells of an $m \times n$ rectangle with numbers whose sum is positive, the figure $\Phi$ can be placed in the rectangle so that the sum of the numbers in the cells of the rectangle covered by $\Phi$ is positive (the figure $\Phi$ may be rotated). Prove that the given rectangle can be covered by the figure $\Phi$ in several layers.
Do there exist $19$ pairwise distinct positive integers with the same sum of digits whose sum equals $1999$?
Integers are placed at all rational points of the real line. Prove that there exists a segment such that the sum of the numbers at its endpoints does not exceed twice the number at its midpoint.

The incircle of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ touches its sides $DA$, $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ at the points $K$, $L$, $M$, $N$, respectively. Let $S_1$, $S_2$, $S_3$, $S_4$ be the incircles of the triangles $AKL$, $BLM$, $CMN$, $DNK$, respectively. The common external tangents, different from the sides of the quadrilateral $ABCD$, are drawn to the circles $S_1$ and $S_2$, $S_2$ and $S_3$, $S_3$ and $S_4$, $S_4$ and $S_1$. Prove that the quadrilateral formed by these four tangents is a rhombus.

In an $n \times n$ square of cells of an infinite chessboard there are $n^2$ counters, one in each cell. A move consists of a counter jumping over an adjacent (by side) counter immediately beyond which there is a free cell. The counter that was jumped over is removed from the board. Prove that a position in which no further moves are possible arises no earlier than after $\left[\frac{n^2}{3}\right]$ moves.
Four positive integers are such that the square of the sum of any two of them is divisible by the product of the remaining two. Prove that at least three of these numbers are equal.

Prove that three convex polygons in the plane cannot be intersected by one line if and only if each polygon can be separated from the other two by a line (i.e. there exists a line such that this polygon and the other two lie on opposite sides of it).

Through the vertex $A$ of a tetrahedron $ABCD$ a plane tangent to its circumscribed sphere is drawn. Prove that the lines of intersection of this plane with the planes of the faces $ABC$, $ACD$ and $ABD$ form six equal angles if and only if $AB \cdot CD = AC \cdot BD = AD \cdot BC$.

A microcircuit has $2000$ contacts; initially any two contacts are joined by a separate wire. The hooligans Vasya and Petya take turns cutting wires: Vasya (who starts) cuts one wire per move, and Petya cuts either two or three wires. The hooligan who cuts the last wire from some contact loses. Which of them wins with correct play?

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ which for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality
$$f(x + y) + f(y + z) + f(z + x) \ge 3f(x + 2y + 3z).$$
Prove that the set of all positive integers can be partitioned into $100$ nonempty subsets so that in any triple $a, b, c$ with $a + 99b = c$ two of the numbers belong to the same subset.

A convex pentagon $ABCDE$ with vertices at lattice points is given in the coordinate plane. Prove that inside or on the boundary of the pentagon $A_1B_1C_1D_1E_1$ (see the figure) there is at least one lattice point.

A sequence of nonnegative numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ is given. For every $k$ from $1$ to $n$ denote by $m_k$ the quantity
$$\max_{l = 1, 2, \dots, k} \frac{a_{k-l+1} + a_{k-l+2} + \dots + a_k}{l}.$$
Prove that for every $\alpha > 0$ the number of those $k$ for which $m_k > \alpha$ is less than $\frac{a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n}{\alpha}$.

Prove the inequality
$$\sin^n 2x + (\sin^n x - \cos^n x)^2 \le 1.$$

A perfect number greater than $28$ is divisible by $7$. Prove that it is divisible by $49$. (A positive integer is called perfect if it equals the sum of all its divisors other than the number itself, for example $6 = 1 + 2 + 3$.)

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is circumscribed about a circle $\omega$. The extensions of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ meet at the point $O$. The circle $\omega_1$ touches the side $BC$ at the point $K$ and the extensions of the sides $AB$ and $CD$; the circle $\omega_2$ touches the side $AD$ at the point $L$ and the extensions of the sides $AB$ and $CD$. It is known that the points $O$, $K$, $L$ lie on one line. Prove that the midpoints of the sides $BC$, $AD$ and the centre of the circle $\omega$ lie on one line.

The cells of a $100 \times 100$ table are coloured in $4$ colours so that every row and every column contains exactly $25$ cells of each colour. Prove that there exist two rows and two columns such that the four cells at their intersections are coloured in four different colours.

Let $2S$ be the total weight of some set of weights. A positive integer $k$ is called average if one can choose $k$ weights from the set whose total weight equals $S$. What is the largest number of average numbers that a set of $100$ weights can have?

Two circles touch internally at the point $N$. The tangent to the inner circle at the point $K$ meets the outer circle at the points $A$ and $B$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $AB$ not containing the point $N$. Prove that the circumradius of triangle $BMK$ does not depend on the choice of the point $K$ on the inner circle.

Two finite sets $P_1$ and $P_2$ of convex polygons are given in the plane such that any two polygons from different sets have a common point, and each of the two sets $P_1$ and $P_2$ contains a pair of disjoint polygons. Prove that there exists a line intersecting all the polygons of both sets.

The participants of a test olympiad were offered $n$ questions. The jury determines the difficulty of each question: a positive integer number of points that participants receive for a correct answer to the question. For a wrong answer $0$ points are given, and all points obtained by a participant are added up. When all participants had handed in their answer sheets, it turned out that the jury could choose the difficulties of the questions so that the places among the participants would be distributed in any prescribed way. What is the largest possible number of participants for which this could happen?

The monic quadratic trinomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ take negative values on disjoint intervals. Prove that there exist positive numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $\alpha f(x) + \beta g(x) > 0$ for every real $x$.
$a$ and $b$ are distinct positive integers such that $ab(a + b)$ is divisible by $a^2 + ab + b^2$. Prove that $|a - b| > \sqrt[3]{ab}$.

A country has $2001$ cities; some pairs of cities are joined by roads, at least one road leaves every city, and no city is joined by roads to all the others. A set of cities $D$ is called dominating if every city not in $D$ is joined by a road to one of the cities of $D$. It is known that every dominating set contains at least $k$ cities. Prove that the country can be divided into $2001 - k$ republics so that no two cities of the same republic are joined by a road.

A sphere with centre in the plane of the base $ABC$ of a tetrahedron $SABC$ passes through the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ and meets the edges $SA$, $SB$ and $SC$ again at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$, respectively. The planes tangent to the sphere at the points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ meet at the point $O$. Prove that $O$ is the circumcentre of the tetrahedron $SA_1B_1C_1$.

Polynomials $P$, $Q$ and $R$ with real coefficients, among which there is a polynomial of degree two and a polynomial of degree three, satisfy the equality
$$P^2 + Q^2 = R^2.$$
Prove that all roots of one of the polynomials of degree three are real.

Several points are marked in the plane. For any three of them there exists a Cartesian coordinate system (i.e. perpendicular axes and a common scale) in which these points have integer coordinates. Prove that there exists a Cartesian coordinate system in which all the marked points have integer coordinates.

Prove that for all $x \in \left(0; \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and positive integers $n > m$ the inequality
$$2|\sin^n x - \cos^n x| \le 3|\sin^m x - \cos^m x|$$
holds.

A town has several squares. Some pairs of squares are joined by one-way streets so that exactly two streets lead out of each square. Prove that the town can be divided into $1014$ districts so that streets join only squares from different districts, and for any two districts all the streets joining them are directed the same way (either all from the first district to the second, or vice versa).

Find the smallest positive integer that can be represented as the sum of $2002$ positive integers with the same sum of digits and also as the sum of $2003$ positive integers with the same sum of digits.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral and $O$ the intersection point of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Let the circumcircles of triangles $ABO$ and $COD$ meet at the point $K$. A point $L$ is such that the triangles $BLC$ and $AKD$ are similar (with vertices in this correspondence). Prove that if the quadrilateral $BLCK$ is convex, then it is tangential.

A finite number of red and blue lines are drawn in the plane, no two of them parallel, such that through every intersection point of two lines of the same colour there passes a line of the other colour. Prove that all the lines pass through one point.

Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ for which the numerator of the irreducible fraction equal to $1 + \frac{1}{2} + \dots + \frac{1}{n}$ is not a power of a prime with a positive integer exponent.

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \tau$ be positive numbers such that for all $x$
$$\sin \alpha x + \sin \beta x = \sin \gamma x + \sin \tau x.$$
Prove that $\alpha = \gamma$ or $\alpha = \tau$.

The diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at the point $O$. Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be the circumcircles of triangles $ABO$ and $CDO$, respectively, and let $O$ and $K$ be the intersection points of the circles $S_1$ and $S_2$. The lines through the point $O$ parallel to the lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet $S_1$ and $S_2$ again at the points $L$ and $M$, respectively. Points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the segments $OL$ and $OM$, respectively, so that $OP : PL = MQ : QO$. Prove that the points $O$, $K$, $P$, $Q$ lie on one circle.

Polynomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ with nonnegative integer coefficients are given, and $m$ is the largest coefficient of the polynomial $f$. It is known that for some positive integers $a < b$ the equalities $f(a) = g(a)$ and $f(b) = g(b)$ hold. Prove that if $b > m$, then the polynomials $f$ and $g$ coincide.

Anya and Borya each had a long strip of paper. The letter A was written on one of them and the letter B on the other. Every minute one of them (not necessarily in turn) appends, on the right or on the left of the word on his or her strip, the word from the other's strip. Prove that after a day the word on Anya's strip can be cut into $2$ parts which, when swapped, give the same word written in reverse order.

The side lengths of a triangle are the roots of a cubic equation with rational coefficients. Prove that the lengths of the altitudes of the triangle are the roots of an equation of degree six with rational coefficients.

Is it possible to place positive integers in the cells of an infinite sheet of squared paper so that for any positive integers $m, n > 100$ the sum of the numbers in any $m \times n$ rectangle of cells is divisible by $m + n$?

A country has $100$ cities, and some pairs of cities are joined by roads. Among any four cities there are at least two roads. It is known that there is no route passing through every city exactly once. Prove that one can choose two cities such that each of the remaining cities is joined by a road to at least one of the two chosen cities.

The sphere inscribed in a tetrahedron $ABCD$ touches its faces $ABC$, $ABD$, $ACD$ and $BCD$ at the points $D_1$, $C_1$, $B_1$ and $A_1$, respectively. Consider the plane equidistant from the point $A$ and the plane $B_1C_1D_1$, and three other planes constructed analogously. Prove that the tetrahedron formed by these four planes has the same circumcentre as the tetrahedron $ABCD$.
Every lattice point of the plane is coloured in one of three colours, and all three colours are present. Prove that there is a right triangle whose vertices have three different colours.

Let $I_A$ and $I_B$ be the centres of the excircles of triangle $ABC$ touching the sides $BC$ and $CA$, respectively, and let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle $\Omega$ of this triangle. Prove that the midpoint of the segment joining the circumcentres of the triangles $I_ACP$ and $I_BCP$ coincides with the centre of the circle $\Omega$.

Polynomials $P(x)$, $Q(x)$ are given. It is known that for some polynomial $R(x, y)$ the equality $P(x) - P(y) = R(x, y)\big(Q(x) - Q(y)\big)$ holds. Prove that there exists a polynomial $S(x)$ such that $P(x) = S(Q(x))$.

A rectangular table has $9$ rows and $2004$ columns. The numbers from $1$ to $2004$ are placed in its cells, each $9$ times. In every column the numbers differ by at most $3$. Find the smallest possible sum of the numbers in the first row.

Let $M = \{x_1, \dots, x_{30}\}$ be a set of $30$ distinct positive numbers, and let $A_n$ ($1 \le n \le 30$) be the sum of all possible products of $n$ distinct elements of the set $M$. Prove that if $A_{15} > A_{10}$, then $A_1 > 1$.

A country has several cities; some pairs of cities are joined by two-way non-stop air routes belonging to $k$ airlines. It is known that any two routes of the same airline have a common endpoint. Prove that all the cities can be divided into $k + 2$ groups so that no two cities of the same group are joined by an air route.
A cross-section of a rectangular box is a hexagon. It is known that this hexagon can be placed in some rectangle $\Pi$. Prove that one of the faces of the box can be placed in the rectangle $\Pi$.

What is the largest finite number of roots that the equation
$$|x - a_1| + \dots + |x - a_{50}| = |x - b_1| + \dots + |x - b_{50}|$$
can have, where $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{50}, b_1, b_2, \dots, b_{50}$ are distinct numbers?

Distinct numbers are written on the backs of $2005$ cards (one on each). With one question one may point to any three cards and learn the set of numbers written on them. What is the smallest number of questions with which one can find out which number is written on each card?

Let $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$ be the points of tangency of the excircles with the corresponding sides of triangle $ABC$. The circumcircles of triangles $A'B'C$, $AB'C'$ and $A'BC'$ meet the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at the points $C_1$, $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively. Prove that the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is similar to the triangle formed by the points of tangency of the incircle of triangle $ABC$ with its sides.

Positive integers $x, y, z$ ($x > 2$, $y > 1$) are such that $x^y + 1 = z^2$. Denote by $p$ the number of distinct prime divisors of $x$ and by $q$ the number of distinct prime divisors of $y$. Prove that $p \ge q + 2$.

Does there exist a bounded function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(1) > 0$ and $f(x)$ satisfies, for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, the inequality
$$f^2(x + y) \ge f^2(x) + 2f(xy) + f^2(y)?$$

Is it possible to place in space $12$ rectangular boxes $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_{12}$, whose edges are parallel to the coordinate axes $Ox$, $Oy$, $Oz$, so that $P_2$ intersects (i.e. has at least one common point with) each of the others except $P_1$ and $P_3$, $P_3$ intersects each of the others except $P_2$ and $P_4$, and so on, $P_{12}$ intersects each of the others except $P_{11}$ and $P_1$, and $P_1$ intersects each of the others except $P_{12}$ and $P_2$? (The surface of a box belongs to it.)

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ with pairwise non-parallel sides is circumscribed about a circle with centre $O$. Prove that the point $O$ coincides with the intersection point of the midlines of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ if and only if $OA \cdot OC = OB \cdot OD$.

$100$ representatives of $25$ countries, $4$ from each country, sit at a round table. Prove that they can be divided into $4$ groups so that each group contains one representative of each country and no two members of the same group sit next to each other at the table.
Prove that $\sin\sqrt{x} < \sqrt{\sin x}$ for $0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
The sum and the product of two purely periodic decimal fractions are purely periodic fractions with period $T$. Prove that the original fractions have periods not exceeding $T$.

In a $49 \times 69$ grid rectangle, all $50 \cdot 70$ vertices of the cells are marked. Two players play the following game: on each move a player joins two of the points with a segment, where no point may be an endpoint of two drawn segments. Segments may have common points. Segments are drawn until the points run out. If afterwards the first player can choose directions on all the drawn segments so that the sum of all the resulting vectors is the zero vector, he wins; otherwise the second player wins. Who wins with correct play?

The angle bisectors $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ of triangle $ABC$ meet at $I$. The line $B_1C_1$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $M$ and $N$. Prove that the circumradius of triangle $MIN$ is twice the circumradius of triangle $ABC$.

Sequences of positive numbers $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ satisfy
$$x_{n+2} = x_n + x_{n+1}^2, \qquad y_{n+2} = y_n^2 + y_{n+1}$$
for all positive integers $n$. Prove that if all the numbers $x_1$, $x_2$, $y_1$, $y_2$ are greater than $1$, then $x_n > y_n$ for some positive integer $n$.

The circle with center $I$ inscribed in the face $ABC$ of a triangular pyramid $SABC$ touches the segments $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. Points $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ are marked on the segments $SA$, $SB$, $SC$ respectively so that $AA' = AD$, $BB' = BE$, $CC' = CF$; $S'$ is the point of the circumsphere of the pyramid diametrically opposite to $S$. It is known that $SI$ is an altitude of the pyramid. Prove that $S'$ is equidistant from $A'$, $B'$, $C'$.

It is known that the polynomial $(x+1)^n - 1$ is divisible by a polynomial
$$P(x) = x^k + c_{k-1}x^{k-1} + c_{k-2}x^{k-2} + \cdots + c_1x + c_0$$
of even degree $k$, all of whose coefficients $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{k-1}$ are odd integers. Prove that $n$ is divisible by $k + 1$.

Several pioneers came to a camp, each of whom has between $50$ and $100$ acquaintances among the others. Prove that the pioneers can be given caps painted in $1331$ colours so that the acquaintances of each pioneer have caps of at least $20$ different colours.

Prove that for $k > 10$, in the product
$$f(x) = \cos x \cos 2x \cos 3x \cdots \cos 2^k x$$
one of the cosines can be replaced by a sine so that the resulting function $f_1(x)$ satisfies $|f_1(x)| \le \dfrac{3}{2^{k+1}}$ for all real $x$.

The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $AC$, $AB$ at $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ respectively. The segment $AA_1$ meets the incircle again at $Q$. A line $\ell$ passes through $A$ parallel to $BC$. The lines $A_1C_1$ and $A_1B_1$ meet $\ell$ at $P$ and $R$ respectively. Prove that $\angle PQR = \angle B_1QC_1$.

A magician and his assistant are going to perform the following trick. A spectator writes an $N$-digit number on the board. The assistant covers two adjacent digits with a black disc. Then the magician enters; his task is to guess both covered digits (and their order). For what smallest $N$ can the magician agree with the assistant so that the trick is guaranteed to succeed?

In an infinite sequence $(x_n)$ the first term $x_1$ is a rational number greater than $1$, and
$$x_{n+1} = x_n + \frac{1}{\lfloor x_n \rfloor}$$
for all positive integers $n$. Prove that the sequence contains an integer.

Two different numbers are written at each vertex of a convex $100$-gon. Prove that one number can be crossed out at each vertex so that the remaining numbers at any two adjacent vertices are different.

Do there exist nonzero numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ such that for every $n > 3$ one can find a polynomial of the form
$$P_n(x) = x^n + \cdots + ax^2 + bx + c$$
having exactly $n$ (not necessarily distinct) integer roots?

A triangular pyramid is given. Lesha wants to choose two of its skew edges and construct balls having these edges as diameters. Can he always choose such a pair so that every point of the pyramid lies in at least one of these balls?

A country has $N$ cities. Some pairs of them are connected by non-stop two-way air routes. It turns out that for every $k$ $(2 \le k \le N)$ and every choice of $k$ cities, the number of air routes between these cities does not exceed $2k - 2$. Prove that all the air routes can be divided between two airlines so that there is no closed air route all of whose flights belong to the same airline.

The numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that the equation $x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has three real roots. Prove that if $-2 \le a + b + c \le 0$, then at least one of these roots belongs to the interval $[0, 2]$.

Petya and Vasya were given identical sets of $N$ weights, in which the masses of any two weights differ by a factor of at most $1.25$. Petya managed to divide all the weights of his set into $10$ groups of equal mass, and Vasya managed to divide all the weights of his set into $11$ groups of equal mass. Find the smallest possible value of $N$.

A finite set $P$ of primes is given. Prove that there is a positive integer $x$ that can be written in the form $x = a^p + b^p$ (with positive integers $a$, $b$) for every $p \in P$, and cannot be written in this form for any prime $p \notin P$.
Each face of a tetrahedron can be placed in a circle of radius $1$. Prove that the whole tetrahedron can be placed in a ball of radius $\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}$.

The numbers from $51$ to $150$ are placed in a $10 \times 10$ table. Can it happen that for every pair of numbers $a$, $b$ in cells sharing a side, at least one of the equations $x^2 - ax + b = 0$ and $x^2 - bx + a = 0$ has two integer roots?

A magician guesses the area of a convex $2008$-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_{2008}$ hidden behind a screen. He names two points on the perimeter of the polygon; the spectators mark these points, draw the line through them and tell the magician the smaller of the two areas of the parts into which this line divides the $2008$-gon. As a point, the magician may name either a vertex or a point dividing a side he names in a ratio he names. Prove that the magician can guess the area of the polygon with $2006$ questions.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the intersections of the rays $BA$ and $CD$, and of $BC$ and $AD$, respectively, and let $H$ be the projection of $D$ onto $PQ$. Prove that $ABCD$ has an incircle if and only if the incircles of triangles $ADP$ and $CDQ$ are seen from $H$ at equal angles.

$2n + 3$ chess players took part in a blitz tournament; each played each other exactly once. A schedule was made so that the games were played one after another and each player rested for at least $n$ games after each game he played. Prove that one of the players who played in the first game also played in the last one.

In a country, some pairs of cities are connected by roads that do not intersect outside cities. In each city a sign shows the minimum length of a route that starts in this city and passes through all the other cities of the country (the route may pass through some cities more than once and need not return to the starting city). Prove that any two numbers on the signs differ by a factor of at most $1.5$.

A sequence $a_1, a_2, \dots$ satisfies $a_1 \in (1, 2)$ and
$$a_{k+1} = a_k + \frac{k}{a_k}$$
for every positive integer $k$. Prove that the sequence cannot contain more than one pair of terms with an integer sum.

In a triangular pyramid $ABCD$, none of the face angles at the vertices is a right angle, and the orthocenters of the triangles $ABC$, $ABD$, $ACD$ lie on a line. Prove that the center of the circumsphere of the pyramid lies in the plane through the midpoints of the edges $AB$, $AC$, $AD$.

All the points $(x, y)$ with integer coordinates such that $x^2 + y^2 \le 10^{10}$ are marked in the plane. Two players play a game, moving alternately. On the first move, the first player puts a token on some marked point and erases it. Then, on each subsequent move, a player moves the token to some other marked point and erases it. The lengths of the moves must always increase; moreover, it is forbidden to move from a point to the point symmetric to it with respect to the center. The player who cannot move loses. Which player can guarantee a win, however the opponent plays?

Let $1 < a \le b \le c$. Prove that
$$\log_a b + \log_b c + \log_c a \le \log_b a + \log_c b + \log_a c.$$

$k$ rooks are placed on some cells of a $10 \times 10$ board, and then all the cells attacked by at least one rook are marked (a rook is considered to attack the cell it stands on). For what largest $k$ can it happen that after removing any rook from the board, at least one marked cell is no longer attacked?

Points $A_1$ and $C_1$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ respectively. The segments $AC_1$ and $CA_1$ meet at $P$. The circumcircles of triangles $AA_1P$ and $CC_1P$ meet again at a point $Q$ inside triangle $ACD$. Prove that $\angle PDA = \angle QBA$.
Positive integers $x, y \in [2, 100]$ are given. Prove that for some positive integer $n$ the number $x^{2^n} + y^{2^n}$ is composite.

Do there exist nonzero real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{10}$ such that
$$\left(a_1 + \frac{1}{a_1}\right) \cdots \left(a_{10} + \frac{1}{a_{10}}\right) = \left(a_1 - \frac{1}{a_1}\right) \cdots \left(a_{10} - \frac{1}{a_{10}}\right)\,?$$

In an $n \times n$ grid table $(n \ge 4)$, $n$ plus signs are placed in the cells of one diagonal and minus signs in all the other cells. It is allowed to change all the signs in some row or in some column to the opposite ones. Prove that after any number of such operations there will be at least $n$ plus signs in the table.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle $\omega$, and its diagonals meet at $K$. Points $M_1$, $M_2$, $M_3$, $M_4$ are the midpoints of the arcs $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ (not containing the other vertices of the quadrilateral) respectively. Points $I_1$, $I_2$, $I_3$, $I_4$ are the incenters of triangles $ABK$, $BCK$, $CDK$, $DAK$ respectively. Prove that the lines $M_1I_1$, $M_2I_2$, $M_3I_3$, $M_4I_4$ are concurrent.

A positive integer $n \ge 3$ is given. For what smallest $k$ is the following statement true: for any $n$ points $A_i = (x_i, y_i)$ in the plane, no three of which are collinear, and any real numbers $c_i$ $(1 \le i \le n)$, there is a polynomial $P(x, y)$ of degree at most $k$ such that $P(x_i, y_i) = c_i$ for all $i = 1, \dots, n$?

(A polynomial in two variables is a function of the form $P(x, y) = a_{0,0} + a_{1,0}x + a_{0,1}y + a_{2,0}x^2 + a_{1,1}xy + a_{0,2}y^2 + \cdots + a_{k,0}x^k + a_{k-1,1}x^{k-1}y + \cdots + a_{0,k}y^k$. The degree of a nonzero monomial $a_{i,j}x^iy^j$ is $i + j$, and the degree of $P(x, y)$ is the largest degree of its monomials.)
A positive integer $n > 1$ is given. Prove that there exist $n$ consecutive positive integers whose product is divisible by all primes not exceeding $2n + 1$ and by no other prime.
Can the $4$ incenters of the faces of a tetrahedron lie in one plane?

A polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $n \ge 3$ has $n$ real roots $x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_n$ with
$$x_2 - x_1 < x_3 - x_2 < \cdots < x_n - x_{n-1}.$$
Prove that the maximum of the function $y = |P(x)|$ on the interval $[x_1, x_n]$ is attained at a point of the interval $[x_{n-1}, x_n]$.

A boarding school teaches $9$ subjects and has $512$ pupils, housed in $256$ double rooms (pupils living in the same room are called roommates). It is known that any two pupils are interested in different sets of subjects (in particular, exactly one pupil is interested in nothing). Prove that all the pupils can be arranged in a circle so that any two roommates stand next to each other, and for any two pupils who are not roommates but stand next to each other, one of them is interested in all the subjects the other is interested in, and in exactly one more.

Positive integers $d$ and $d'$ with $d' > d$ are divisors of a positive integer $n$. Prove that
$$d' > d + \frac{d^2}{n}.$$

On the side $BC$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ $(\angle A < 90^\circ)$ a point $T$ is marked so that triangle $ATD$ is acute. Let $O_1$, $O_2$, $O_3$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABT$, $DAT$ and $CDT$ respectively (see the figure). Prove that the orthocenter of triangle $O_1O_2O_3$ lies on the line $AD$.
